---
title: "Cursor files"
description: Understand the file that holds a recording's pointer, clicks and keys, how it follows its movie, and how to fix it when it doesn't.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A cursor file sits beside a screen recording and holds what the pointer did, so Frame Job can draw and restyle the pointer later. You rarely touch one. This page is for when a movie has moved, lost its file or picked up the wrong one.

<AtAGlance
  where="Media tab ▸ Cursor"
  tools={['set_media_cursor', 'get_cursor_events']}
/>

## What a cursor file holds

Every recording of a display, a window or a picked window writes a cursor file, whichever **Cursor:** option you chose. A camera on its own and a voice-over don't, because they have no pointer. The file has the movie's name, ending in `.fjcursor`, and sits in the same folder:

```
Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.mov
Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.fjcursor
```

A paused recording has one movie per stretch between pauses, and each movie gets its own file.

The file is plain text and records:

- Where the pointer was, about 120 times a second.
- Every click and every scroll.
- How the recorded area sat on the screen, so a window that moved mid-recording still lines up.
- With [Record shortcuts](/recording/record-shortcuts/) on, the shortcuts you pressed and when you typed. A typed key is stored as a time only, never as a character.

It holds no pictures of the pointer, so the pointer you see drawn is [Frame Job's arrow](/recording/cursor-settings/#choose-the-pointers-style).

With **Cursor:** set to **In the picture**, the pointer is drawn into the movie as well and the file says so. Frame Job then draws nothing over the clip, and the clip has no **Cursor** section. The file is still used for its clicks and keys.

[Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/), [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/), [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) and [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) all read this file.

## How the file follows its movie

Frame Job keeps a movie and its cursor file together wherever it can. Keep them in the same folder with the same name when you move them by hand, and an import will find the file.

### When a recording lands

Each stretch's movie gets its own cursor file attached as it lands. You don't need to do anything.

### When you import a movie

Importing a movie with **File ▸ Add Media…**, a drop on the window, or by opening it looks beside the movie for a file with the same name ending in `.fjcursor`. Frame Job takes it only if it reads as a cursor file and was made for a movie of exactly this size.

A file that's missing, damaged or made for another size is left alone and the movie imports without it. Frame Job says nothing about it, so if a recording arrives with no **Cursor** section, check the [Media tab](#see-a-movies-cursor-file).

A WebM or Matroska file is copied into a movie as it imports, and that copy isn't looked beside.

### When you relink a movie

[Relinking](/projects/relink-media/) takes the cursor file beside the new movie. If there's none, the media keeps the cursor file it already had, as long as that file is still there and the new movie is the same size. Otherwise the media has no cursor file after the relink, and you can attach one with **Locate…**.

### When you consolidate

[Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/) copies each cursor file into the package beside its movie, and a moved package finds it there again when you open it.

If a cursor file is missing, Consolidate leaves it alone and its report says so, for example "1 cursor file was missing and left alone." If a copy fails, the media goes on pointing at the original file. A movie that's missing is left alone along with its cursor file.

## See a movie's cursor file

Select a video in the **Media** tab's list and read its **Cursor** section. The section appears once the project has a video with a picture.

| The section says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Select a video in the list" | Nothing that can carry a cursor file is selected. |
| "No cursor file" | This video has none attached. |
| The file's name | The file is attached and on disk. |
| The file's name, then "— missing" | The file is attached but has gone from where it was. |

## Attach or re-point a cursor file

Use **Locate…** to give a video its cursor file, or to point it at one that has moved.

<Steps>

1. Select the video in the **Media** tab's list.

2. In the **Cursor** section, choose **Locate…**.

3. Choose the `.fjcursor` file recorded with this movie.

</Steps>

Frame Job runs the same check as an import: the file must read as a cursor file made for a movie of exactly this size. If it passes, that's one undo step called "Locate Cursor File". If it doesn't, an alert titled "The cursor file was not attached" gives the reason and nothing changes. For example:

- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: its movie_size is 3024 × 1964 and the movie is 1920 × 1080."
- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: this is not a Frame Job cursor file…"

A cursor file from a newer version of Frame Job is refused the same way, and the alert says which version it is.

## Forget a cursor file

Choose **Remove** in the **Cursor** section. The video stops using the file, as one undo step called "Remove Cursor File". The file itself stays on disk, so you can choose **Locate…** to bring it back. **Remove** is dimmed for a video with no cursor file.

## When a cursor file has a problem

A cursor problem never fails a recording or an export. You always get the movie, and Frame Job tells you what's missing.

### While recording

If a stretch's cursor file can't be written, the recording still lands and the panel's note says why, naming the file:

| The note says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "The cursor file *name* could not be written…", "…was not kept…", "…could not be put in place…" | The file couldn't be saved, or didn't pass Frame Job's own read-back. No file was left behind. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: no cursor was captured for it." | Nothing was captured for this stretch. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: the screen never reported its start, so its times have nothing to count from." | Without a start time, the pointer can't be matched to the picture. |
| "The cursor file for *name* has only the geometry the screen had when it began…" | A file exists, but a move or resize of what was recorded after the start isn't in it, so the pointer can sit in the wrong place after that. |

A stretch recorded **Separate** with no cursor file has no pointer at all, because it isn't in the movie and there's nothing to draw it from. The note ends "The pointer is not in the movie either: it was recorded Separate."

### While exporting

If a cursor file can't be drawn, because it's missing or damaged, the clip exports without a pointer and the export finishes as normal. The export's finish line counts the problem, for example "1 cursor warning (hover for details).", and hovering lists each one. The [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) shows the count on the job's row, with the same list in its tooltip:

> The cursor of media 3 is not drawn: …

### In the preview

A missing or damaged cursor file draws no pointer, and the preview says nothing. Check the **Media** tab, and use **Locate…** if the name reads "— missing".

## Good to know

- Moving a cursor file away doesn't take the clip's **Cursor** section with it. The section stays, and nothing is drawn until the file is back.
- Removing or re-pointing a cursor file doesn't touch the [settings on its clips](/recording/cursor-settings/). They wait for the next file.

## With an agent

An agent can read what a cursor file holds, which the app doesn't show you as a list. `get_cursor_events` answers a recording's clicks, scrolls, shortcuts and stretches of typing, and the pointer's path if asked. It reads in the file's own time or in a clip's, and it can give each click's place in the clip's picture, ready for a zoom. It edits nothing, runs on your Mac and needs no key.

It won't read a clip that plays reversed, though it can read that clip's media, and it needs a media with a cursor file that's still on disk.

`set_media_cursor` attaches, moves or removes a file as **Locate…** and **Remove** do, under the same check. See [Tools: recording and screencasts](/mcp/tools-recording/).

## Related

- [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/)
- [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/)
- [Recording files and formats](/recording/files-and-formats/)
- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)
- [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/)

- With [Record shortcuts](/recording/record-shortcuts/) on, the shortcuts you pressed and when you typed. A typed key is stored as a time only, never as a character.

It holds no pictures of the pointer, so the pointer you see drawn is [Frame Job's arrow](/recording/cursor-settings/#choose-the-pointers-style).

With **Cursor:** set to **In the picture**, the pointer is drawn into the movie as well and the file says so. Frame Job then draws nothing over the clip, and the clip has no **Cursor** section. The file is still used for its clicks and keys.

[Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/), [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/), [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) and [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) all read this file.

## How the file follows its movie

Frame Job keeps a movie and its cursor file together wherever it can. Keep them in the same folder with the same name when you move them by hand, and an import will find the file.

### When a recording lands

Each stretch's movie gets its own cursor file attached as it lands. You don't need to do anything.

### When you import a movie

Importing a movie with **File ▸ Add Media…**, a drop on the window, or by opening it looks beside the movie for a file with the same name ending in `.fjcursor`. Frame Job takes it only if it reads as a cursor file and was made for a movie of exactly this size.

A file that's missing, damaged or made for another size is left alone and the movie imports without it. Frame Job says nothing about it, so if a recording arrives with no **Cursor** section, check the [Media tab](#see-a-movies-cursor-file).

A WebM or Matroska file is copied into a movie as it imports, and that copy isn't looked beside.

### When you relink a movie

[Relinking](/projects/relink-media/) takes the cursor file beside the new movie. If there's none, the media keeps the cursor file it already had, as long as that file is still there and the new movie is the same size. Otherwise the media has no cursor file after the relink, and you can attach one with **Locate…**.

### When you consolidate

[Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/) copies each cursor file into the package beside its movie, and a moved package finds it there again when you open it.

If a cursor file is missing, Consolidate leaves it alone and its report says so, for example "1 cursor file was missing and left alone." If a copy fails, the media goes on pointing at the original file. A movie that's missing is left alone along with its cursor file.

## See a movie's cursor file

Select a video in the **Media** tab's list and read its **Cursor** section. The section appears once the project has a video with a picture.

| The section says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Select a video in the list" | Nothing that can carry a cursor file is selected. |
| "No cursor file" | This video has none attached. |
| The file's name | The file is attached and on disk. |
| The file's name, then "— missing" | The file is attached but has gone from where it was. |

## Attach or re-point a cursor file

Use **Locate…** to give a video its cursor file, or to point it at one that has moved.

<Steps>

1. Select the video in the **Media** tab's list.

2. In the **Cursor** section, choose **Locate…**.

3. Choose the `.fjcursor` file recorded with this movie.

</Steps>

Frame Job runs the same check as an import: the file must read as a cursor file made for a movie of exactly this size. If it passes, that's one undo step called "Locate Cursor File". If it doesn't, an alert titled "The cursor file was not attached" gives the reason and nothing changes. For example:

- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: its movie_size is 3024 × 1964 and the movie is 1920 × 1080."
- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: this is not a Frame Job cursor file…"

A cursor file from a newer version of Frame Job is refused the same way, and the alert says which version it is.

## Forget a cursor file

Choose **Remove** in the **Cursor** section. The video stops using the file, as one undo step called "Remove Cursor File". The file itself stays on disk, so you can choose **Locate…** to bring it back. **Remove** is dimmed for a video with no cursor file.

## When a cursor file has a problem

A cursor problem never fails a recording or an export. You always get the movie, and Frame Job tells you what's missing.

### While recording

If a stretch's cursor file can't be written, the recording still lands and the panel's note says why, naming the file:

| The note says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "The cursor file *name* could not be written…", "…was not kept…", "…could not be put in place…" | The file couldn't be saved, or didn't pass Frame Job's own read-back. No file was left behind. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: no cursor was captured for it." | Nothing was captured for this stretch. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: the screen never reported its start, so its times have nothing to count from." | Without a start time, the pointer can't be matched to the picture. |
| "The cursor file for *name* has only the geometry the screen had when it began…" | A file exists, but a move or resize of what was recorded after the start isn't in it, so the pointer can sit in the wrong place after that. |

A stretch recorded **Separate** with no cursor file has no pointer at all, because it isn't in the movie and there's nothing to draw it from. The note ends "The pointer is not in the movie either: it was recorded Separate."

### While exporting

If a cursor file can't be drawn, because it's missing or damaged, the clip exports without a pointer and the export finishes as normal. The export's finish line counts the problem, for example "1 cursor warning (hover for details).", and hovering lists each one. The [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) shows the count on the job's row, with the same list in its tooltip:

> The cursor of media 3 is not drawn: …

### In the preview

A missing or damaged cursor file draws no pointer, and the preview says nothing. Check the **Media** tab, and use **Locate…** if the name reads "— missing".

## Good to know

- Moving a cursor file away doesn't take the clip's **Cursor** section with it. The section stays, and nothing is drawn until the file is back.
- Removing or re-pointing a cursor file doesn't touch the [settings on its clips](/recording/cursor-settings/). They wait for the next file.

## With an agent

An agent can read what a cursor file holds, which the app doesn't show you as a list. `get_cursor_events` answers a recording's clicks, scrolls, shortcuts and stretches of typing, and the pointer's path if asked. It reads in the file's own time or in a clip's, and it can give each click's place in the clip's picture, ready for a zoom. It edits nothing, runs on your Mac and needs no key.

It won't read a clip that plays reversed, though it can read that clip's media, and it needs a media with a cursor file that's still on disk.

`set_media_cursor` attaches, moves or removes a file as **Locate…** and **Remove** do, under the same check. See [Tools: recording and screencasts](/mcp/tools-recording/).

## Related

- [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/)
- [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/)
- [Recording files and formats](/recording/files-and-formats/)
- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)
- [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/)

---
title: "Record shortcuts"
description: Note the keyboard shortcuts you press during a screen recording, and when you type, without ever recording what you type.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Record shortcuts notes each keyboard shortcut you press during a screen recording, and when you type, so Frame Job can show those shortcuts on screen and speed up the typing afterwards. It never records what you type.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ New Recording…"
  where="New Recording panel ▸ Record shortcuts"
  tools={['record_screen', 'get_cursor_events']}
  needs="macOS's Input Monitoring permission, and a display or a window as the source."
/>

## Turn it on

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ New Recording…**.

2. Set **Source:** to a display or a window.

3. Tick **Record shortcuts**. It's off to begin with, and the panel remembers your choice for the next recording.

4. Press **Record**. The first time, you'll need to [grant Input Monitoring](#grant-input-monitoring).

</Steps>

The box is greyed out for **Camera** and **Microphone Only**, which have no screen to go with the keys. It keeps its tick for when you go back to a screen source.

While keys are being recorded, the [menu-bar item](/recording/menu-bar-item/) shows a keyboard mark beside the time, and its menu opens with a dimmed "Recording keyboard shortcuts" row. Everything lands in the recording's [cursor files](/recording/cursor-files/).

## Grant Input Monitoring

Recording keys needs macOS's **Input Monitoring** permission. macOS shows no prompt for it, and Frame Job isn't in that pane's list until you add it, so pressing **Record** without the permission stops the recording from starting and opens System Settings for you.

<Steps>

1. Press **Record**. System Settings opens at **Privacy & Security ▸ Input Monitoring**, and the panel's note says what to do.

2. Turn Frame Job on. If it isn't in the list, add it with **+**.

3. Back in the panel, press **Record** again. You don't need to relaunch.

</Steps>

Frame Job asks for this after Screen Recording, and before the camera and the microphone. See [Recording permissions](/recording/permissions/) for all of them, and for what changes if you started Frame Job from a terminal.

## What counts as a shortcut

A key press is a shortcut when you hold:

- <kbd>⌘</kbd> or <kbd>⌃</kbd> with any key.
- <kbd>⌥</kbd> with an arrow, Delete, Forward Delete, Return, Enter, Tab or Esc.

<kbd>⇧</kbd> on its own never makes a shortcut, and neither does <kbd>⌥</kbd> with any other key, because that types a character: <kbd>⌥E</kbd> starts an é.

A shortcut is stored with its keys spelled out, such as `cmd+shift+4`. The modifiers come first, in the order `cmd`, `ctrl`, `opt`, `shift`. The key comes last: a named key such as `return`, `tab`, `space`, `left` or `f5`, or otherwise the character the key types with no modifier, in lower case. `+` itself is spelled `plus`.

## What happens to everything else

Every other key press is stored as a typing mark, which is a moment in time and nothing more. It doesn't say which key it was. Frame Job doesn't read the character of a typed key at all, and there's no mode that records what you type.

A key held down until it repeats gives typing marks too, even if it began as a shortcut. Holding <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> is one shortcut and then a run of typing marks.

## When nothing is recorded

Nothing at all is recorded while any app holds secure input, as a password field does: no shortcut, and not even a typing mark.

A password field that doesn't turn on secure input is different. A `sudo` prompt in Terminal with **Secure Keyboard Entry** off is recorded as typing marks only, with no characters.

Keys you press while the recording is [paused](/recording/pause-and-stop/) aren't recorded.

:::caution
The keys stay out of the file, but the movie is still a picture of your screen. A password that shows on screen as you type it is in the recording.
:::

## What you can do with the keys

| Feature | What it uses | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) | The shortcuts, shown on screen as you pressed them. | **Clip ▸ Add Shortcut Overlays**, or **Show shortcuts** in the panel |
| [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) | The typing marks, to find the stretches to speed up. | **Clip ▸ Speed Up Typing…**, or **Speed up typing** in the panel |
| [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/) | The typing marks, to zoom in where you typed. | **Zoom on typing** in **Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…** |

**Show shortcuts** and **Speed up typing** are in the panel's **When it lands:** rows, and they're greyed out unless **Record shortcuts** is ticked, because the cursor file would have no keys for them to use.

## With an agent

`record_screen` records keys when it's asked for them, but it never asks macOS for the permission. Without Input Monitoring it won't start, and it names the System Settings pane, so someone has to grant it in the panel first. It won't record keys from a voice-over or a camera on its own. `get_cursor_events` reads the shortcuts and stretches of typing back. See [Tools: recording and screencasts](/mcp/tools-recording/).

## Related

- [The recorder panel](/recording/recorder-panel/)
- [Recording permissions](/recording/permissions/)
- [Cursor files](/recording/cursor-files/)
- [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/)
- [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/)

content.content:
# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a

<system-reminder>
Contents of /Users/kevingalligan/devel/framejob/.claude/worktrees/help-docs/docs/site/CLAUDE.md:

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>

---
title: "Style the recorded cursor"
description: Change how a recording's pointer looks after you've recorded it, from its size and path to when it hides and a ring on every click.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

When a screen recording keeps its pointer out of the movie, Frame Job draws the pointer for you, so you can restyle it long after you stopped recording. The **Cursor** section makes it bigger, calms a shaky path, hides it when it rests and puts a ring on every click.

<AtAGlance
  where="Clip tab ▸ Picture ▸ Cursor"
  tools={['set_video', 'paste_attributes']}
  needs="A recording whose cursor file isn't already in the picture. That's every recording made with Cursor set to Separate, the default."
/>

## Find the Cursor section

Select a recording's clip, open the **Clip** tab's **Picture** sub-tab and look after **Background**. The section starts shut. Its header sums up what's set: **off**, **on** or **arrow**, with **+ ripples** when clicks ripple.

The section is there only when every selected clip comes from a movie with a [cursor file](/recording/cursor-files/) that the picture doesn't already show:

- A recording made with **Cursor:** set to **In the picture** has no section, because the pointer is part of the movie and would otherwise be drawn twice. See [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/).
- A movie with no cursor file has no section. If the file exists but didn't come along, [attach it with Locate…](/recording/cursor-files/#attach-or-re-point-a-cursor-file).
- A selection that also holds any other kind of clip has no section.

A freeze frame of a recording has the section too, with the pointer held where it was on that frame.

Each row is its own undo step. If the selected clips disagree about a row, it shows as mixed.

## Tidy the pointer in one click

Choose **Polish** at the bottom of the section. It sets **Smoothing** to **Medium** and **Hide when idle** to **3 s**, as one undo step called "Polish Cursor". Nothing else changes, and you can adjust either row afterwards.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Show cursor** | Draws the pointer. | On | On, off |
| **Size** | How big the pointer is drawn. | 100 % | 25–800 % |
| **Style** | Which pointer is drawn. | As recorded | As recorded, Arrow |
| **Smoothing** | Calms a shaky path. | Off | Off, Light, Medium, Strong |
| **Hide when idle** | Fades out a resting pointer. | Never | Never, 1, 2, 3, 5 or 10 s |
| **Clicks** | Draws a ring out of every click. | None | None, Ripple |
| **Ripple color** | The ring's colour, with opacity. | White at 80 % | Any colour |
| **Ripple size** | How big the ring grows. | 100 % | 25–400 % |

## Show or resize the pointer

Untick **Show cursor** to draw no pointer on this clip. Click rings are separate, so with **Clicks** set to **Ripple** the rings still draw without a pointer. That's useful when you want to show where someone clicked and nothing else.

**Size** has quick picks at 50, 100, 150, 200 and 400 %. Its slider runs to 400 %, and you can type up to 800 % in the field.

## Choose the pointer's style

**Style** offers **As recorded** and **Arrow**. Frame Job's recordings don't store pictures of the pointer, so both choices draw Frame Job's arrow, and a pointer that was an I-beam or a hand on screen is drawn as the arrow too. The only difference you'll see is that the section's header reads **arrow** rather than **on**.

Frame Job's arrow is a black arrow with a white outline, 14 by 21 points at 100 %. It's drawn at the recording's own pixel density and redrawn for each **Size** rather than stretched, so it stays crisp.

## Calm a shaky path

**Smoothing** irons out the wobble in the pointer's path, from **Light** through **Medium** to **Strong**. The pointer still reaches every click exactly, at the moment of the click, and a pause stays a pause.

## Hide a resting pointer

**Hide when idle** fades the pointer out after the time you pick with no movement and no mouse press. Scrolling and typing don't count as activity. The fade takes 0.2 s, and the pointer comes back 0.15 s before it next moves or clicks, so it's already there when it sets off.

## Show clicks

Set **Clicks** to **Ripple** to draw a ring growing out of every press of a mouse button. A ring lasts 0.45 s, growing quickly at first and fading as it goes, and up to four can show at once. At 100 % it reaches 24 points from the click.

**Ripple color** and **Ripple size** are live only while **Clicks** is **Ripple**. **Ripple size** has quick picks at 50, 100, 150 and 200 %.

**Clicks** starts at **None**, unless the recording was made with **Show Clicks:** on and **Cursor:** set to **Separate**. Those clips land with **Ripple** already set.

## Put everything back

**Reset** in the section's header appears once something differs from its default. It sets all eight rows back to the defaults in the table, as one undo step called "Reset Cursor".

## Change the pointer part-way through a clip

Select an [action](/motion/actions/) on the clip and the section edits that action instead of the whole clip:

| Rows | With an action selected |
| --- | --- |
| **Size**, **Ripple size** | Animate across the action. |
| **Show cursor**, **Style**, **Clicks**, **Ripple color** | Switch at the action's end. |
| **Smoothing**, **Hide when idle** | Always change the clip itself. Their rows show ⊘. |

**Polish** also changes the clip itself, whatever is selected. **Reset** with an action selected puts the first six rows back at that action's end, and **Smoothing** and **Hide when idle** back on the clip.

The first time you change one of the action rows on a clip with no cursor settings of its own, Frame Job stores the defaults on the clip in the same step. That's what lets **Size** and **Ripple size** animate from 100 % instead of jumping.

## Copy the settings to another clip

**Edit ▸ Paste Attributes** (<kbd>⌥⌘V</kbd>) carries a clip's cursor settings to another clip, along with the rest of its picture settings. The settings are replaced as a whole, so pasting from a clip whose cursor you never changed puts the target's back to the defaults. See [Paste Attributes](/editing/paste-attributes/).

## Streak a moving pointer

With the clip's **Motion Blur** above 0, in the **Transform** section, a moving pointer is streaked along its path across the shutter. That happens even when the clip itself stands still, so a fast flick across the screen looks natural in an otherwise static recording. A still pointer and the click rings stay sharp.

The streak shows in the preview, in rendered frames and in every export. A clip that [motion blur](/motion/motion-blur/) draws sharp keeps its pointer sharp, and so does a freeze frame.

## How the pointer sits in the picture

The pointer is drawn inside its clip, as if it were part of the movie. So it follows the clip's zooms, placement and crop, it takes the clip's grade, and the preview, rendered frames and exports all agree. In an HLG project the pointer and its rings are lifted to match the picture.

It also follows the clip's time. Change the clip's speed and the pointer speeds up with it. [Reverse the clip](/speed/reverse/) and the pointer plays backwards too.

## Good to know

- A cursor file loads in the background and never holds up the preview. Until it's ready the frame draws without the pointer, then redraws with it. Changing **Smoothing** can do the same for a moment, because the new path has to be worked out. Rendered frames and exports wait for the file.
- **Hide when idle** and the ring's 0.45 s count in the recording's own time, so on a clip at 2× they pass twice as fast.
- [Splitting](/editing/split/) a clip or making a freeze frame keeps the clip's own **Smoothing** and **Hide when idle**, even from inside an action.
- Paste onto a clip with no cursor file and the settings are kept but nothing is drawn.
- If a cursor file is missing or can't be read, the clip draws with no pointer. See [When a cursor file has a problem](/recording/cursor-files/#when-a-cursor-file-has-a-problem).

## With an agent

`set_video` sets the same eight values, and it isn't held to the pop-ups' steps: **Smoothing** can be any value from 0 to 1, and **Hide when idle** anything from 0.5 to 30 seconds. See [Tools: picture and grade](/mcp/tools-set-video/).

## Related

- [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/)
- [Cursor files](/recording/cursor-files/)
- [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/)
- [Motion blur](/motion/motion-blur/)

---
title: "Cursor files"
description: Understand the file that holds a recording's pointer, clicks and keys, how it follows its movie, and how to fix it when it doesn't.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

A cursor file sits beside a screen recording and holds what the pointer did, so Frame Job can draw and restyle the pointer later. You rarely touch one. This page is for when a movie has moved, lost its file or picked up the wrong one.

<AtAGlance
  where="Media tab ▸ Cursor"
  tools={['set_media_cursor', 'get_cursor_events']}
/>

## What a cursor file holds

Every recording of a display, a window or a picked window writes a cursor file, whichever **Cursor:** option you chose. A camera on its own and a voice-over don't, because they have no pointer. The file has the movie's name, ending in `.fjcursor`, and sits in the same folder:

```
Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.mov
Screen Recording 2026-09-10 at 14.03.22.fjcursor
```

A paused recording has one movie per stretch between pauses, and each movie gets its own file.

The file is plain text and records:

- Where the pointer was, about 120 times a second.
- Every click and every scroll.
- How the recorded area sat on the screen, so a window that moved mid-recording still lines up.
- With [Record shortcuts](/recording/record-shortcuts/) on, the shortcuts you pressed and when you typed. A typed key is stored as a time only, never as a character.

It holds no pictures of the pointer, so the pointer you see drawn is [Frame Job's arrow](/recording/cursor-settings/#choose-the-pointers-style).

With **Cursor:** set to **In the picture**, the pointer is drawn into the movie as well and the file says so. Frame Job then draws nothing over the clip, and the clip has no **Cursor** section. The file is still used for its clicks and keys.

[Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/), [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/), [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) and [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) all read this file.

## How the file follows its movie

Frame Job keeps a movie and its cursor file together wherever it can. Keep them in the same folder with the same name when you move them by hand, and an import will find the file.

### When a recording lands

Each stretch's movie gets its own cursor file attached as it lands. You don't need to do anything.

### When you import a movie

Importing a movie with **File ▸ Add Media…**, a drop on the window, or by opening it looks beside the movie for a file with the same name ending in `.fjcursor`. Frame Job takes it only if it reads as a cursor file and was made for a movie of exactly this size.

A file that's missing, damaged or made for another size is left alone and the movie imports without it. Frame Job says nothing about it, so if a recording arrives with no **Cursor** section, check the [Media tab](#see-a-movies-cursor-file).

A WebM or Matroska file is copied into a movie as it imports, and that copy isn't looked beside.

### When you relink a movie

[Relinking](/projects/relink-media/) takes the cursor file beside the new movie. If there's none, the media keeps the cursor file it already had, as long as that file is still there and the new movie is the same size. Otherwise the media has no cursor file after the relink, and you can attach one with **Locate…**.

### When you consolidate

[Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/) copies each cursor file into the package beside its movie, and a moved package finds it there again when you open it.

If a cursor file is missing, Consolidate leaves it alone and its report says so, for example "1 cursor file was missing and left alone." If a copy fails, the media goes on pointing at the original file. A movie that's missing is left alone along with its cursor file.

## See a movie's cursor file

Select a video in the **Media** tab's list and read its **Cursor** section. The section appears once the project has a video with a picture.

| The section says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Select a video in the list" | Nothing that can carry a cursor file is selected. |
| "No cursor file" | This video has none attached. |
| The file's name | The file is attached and on disk. |
| The file's name, then "— missing" | The file is attached but has gone from where it was. |

## Attach or re-point a cursor file

Use **Locate…** to give a video its cursor file, or to point it at one that has moved.

<Steps>

1. Select the video in the **Media** tab's list.

2. In the **Cursor** section, choose **Locate…**.

3. Choose the `.fjcursor` file recorded with this movie.

</Steps>

Frame Job runs the same check as an import: the file must read as a cursor file made for a movie of exactly this size. If it passes, that's one undo step called "Locate Cursor File". If it doesn't, an alert titled "The cursor file was not attached" gives the reason and nothing changes. For example:

- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: its movie_size is 3024 × 1964 and the movie is 1920 × 1080."
- "The cursor file *name* was not attached: this is not a Frame Job cursor file…"

A cursor file from a newer version of Frame Job is refused the same way, and the alert says which version it is.

## Forget a cursor file

Choose **Remove** in the **Cursor** section. The video stops using the file, as one undo step called "Remove Cursor File". The file itself stays on disk, so you can choose **Locate…** to bring it back. **Remove** is dimmed for a video with no cursor file.

## When a cursor file has a problem

A cursor problem never fails a recording or an export. You always get the movie, and Frame Job tells you what's missing.

### While recording

If a stretch's cursor file can't be written, the recording still lands and the panel's note says why, naming the file:

| The note says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "The cursor file *name* could not be written…", "…was not kept…", "…could not be put in place…" | The file couldn't be saved, or didn't pass Frame Job's own read-back. No file was left behind. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: no cursor was captured for it." | Nothing was captured for this stretch. |
| "The cursor file for *name* was not written: the screen never reported its start, so its times have nothing to count from." | Without a start time, the pointer can't be matched to the picture. |
| "The cursor file for *name* has only the geometry the screen had when it began…" | A file exists, but a move or resize of what was recorded after the start isn't in it, so the pointer can sit in the wrong place after that. |

A stretch recorded **Separate** with no cursor file has no pointer at all, because it isn't in the movie and there's nothing to draw it from. The note ends "The pointer is not in the movie either: it was recorded Separate."

### While exporting

If a cursor file can't be drawn, because it's missing or damaged, the clip exports without a pointer and the export finishes as normal. The export's finish line counts the problem, for example "1 cursor warning (hover for details).", and hovering lists each one. The [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) shows the count on the job's row, with the same list in its tooltip:

> The cursor of media 3 is not drawn: …

### In the preview

A missing or damaged cursor file draws no pointer, and the preview says nothing. Check the **Media** tab, and use **Locate…** if the name reads "— missing".

## Good to know

- Moving a cursor file away doesn't take the clip's **Cursor** section with it. The section stays, and nothing is drawn until the file is back.
- Removing or re-pointing a cursor file doesn't touch the [settings on its clips](/recording/cursor-settings/). They wait for the next file.

## With an agent

An agent can read what a cursor file holds, which the app doesn't show you as a list. `get_cursor_events` answers a recording's clicks, scrolls, shortcuts and stretches of typing, and the pointer's path if asked. It reads in the file's own time or in a clip's, and it can give each click's place in the clip's picture, ready for a zoom. It edits nothing, runs on your Mac and needs no key.

It won't read a clip that plays reversed, though it can read that clip's media, and it needs a media with a cursor file that's still on disk.

`set_media_cursor` attaches, moves or removes a file as **Locate…** and **Remove** do, under the same check. See [Tools: recording and screencasts](/mcp/tools-recording/).

## Related

- [The cursor in a recording](/recording/cursor/)
- [Style the recorded cursor](/recording/cursor-settings/)
- [Recording files and formats](/recording/files-and-formats/)
- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)
- [Consolidate Media](/projects/consolidate-media/)

---
title: "Record shortcuts"
description: Note the keyboard shortcuts you press during a screen recording, and when you type, without ever recording what you type.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Record shortcuts notes each keyboard shortcut you press during a screen recording, and when you type, so Frame Job can show those shortcuts on screen and speed up the typing afterwards. It never records what you type.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ New Recording…"
  where="New Recording panel ▸ Record shortcuts"
  tools={['record_screen', 'get_cursor_events']}
  needs="macOS's Input Monitoring permission, and a display or a window as the source."
/>

## Turn it on

<Steps>

1. Choose **File ▸ New Recording…**.

2. Set **Source:** to a display or a window.

3. Tick **Record shortcuts**. It's off to begin with, and the panel remembers your choice for the next recording.

4. Press **Record**. The first time, you'll need to [grant Input Monitoring](#grant-input-monitoring).

</Steps>

The box is greyed out for **Camera** and **Microphone Only**, which have no screen to go with the keys. It keeps its tick for when you go back to a screen source.

While keys are being recorded, the [menu-bar item](/recording/menu-bar-item/) shows a keyboard mark beside the time, and its menu opens with a dimmed "Recording keyboard shortcuts" row. Everything lands in the recording's [cursor files](/recording/cursor-files/).

## Grant Input Monitoring

Recording keys needs macOS's **Input Monitoring** permission. macOS shows no prompt for it, and Frame Job isn't in that pane's list until you add it, so pressing **Record** without the permission stops the recording from starting and opens System Settings for you.

<Steps>

1. Press **Record**. System Settings opens at **Privacy & Security ▸ Input Monitoring**, and the panel's note says what to do.

2. Turn Frame Job on. If it isn't in the list, add it with **+**.

3. Back in the panel, press **Record** again. You don't need to relaunch.

</Steps>

Frame Job asks for this after Screen Recording, and before the camera and the microphone. See [Recording permissions](/recording/permissions/) for all of them, and for what changes if you started Frame Job from a terminal.

## What counts as a shortcut

A key press is a shortcut when you hold:

- <kbd>⌘</kbd> or <kbd>⌃</kbd> with any key.
- <kbd>⌥</kbd> with an arrow, Delete, Forward Delete, Return, Enter, Tab or Esc.

<kbd>⇧</kbd> on its own never makes a shortcut, and neither does <kbd>⌥</kbd> with any other key, because that types a character: <kbd>⌥E</kbd> starts an é.

A shortcut is stored with its keys spelled out, such as `cmd+shift+4`. The modifiers come first, in the order `cmd`, `ctrl`, `opt`, `shift`. The key comes last: a named key such as `return`, `tab`, `space`, `left` or `f5`, or otherwise the character the key types with no modifier, in lower case. `+` itself is spelled `plus`.

## What happens to everything else

Every other key press is stored as a typing mark, which is a moment in time and nothing more. It doesn't say which key it was. Frame Job doesn't read the character of a typed key at all, and there's no mode that records what you type.

A key held down until it repeats gives typing marks too, even if it began as a shortcut. Holding <kbd>⌘Z</kbd> is one shortcut and then a run of typing marks.

## When nothing is recorded

Nothing at all is recorded while any app holds secure input, as a password field does: no shortcut, and not even a typing mark.

A password field that doesn't turn on secure input is different. A `sudo` prompt in Terminal with **Secure Keyboard Entry** off is recorded as typing marks only, with no characters.

Keys you press while the recording is [paused](/recording/pause-and-stop/) aren't recorded.

:::caution
The keys stay out of the file, but the movie is still a picture of your screen. A password that shows on screen as you type it is in the recording.
:::

## What you can do with the keys

| Feature | What it uses | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Shortcut overlays](/recording/shortcut-overlays/) | The shortcuts, shown on screen as you pressed them. | **Clip ▸ Add Shortcut Overlays**, or **Show shortcuts** in the panel |
| [Speed Up Typing](/recording/speed-up-typing/) | The typing marks, to find the stretches to speed up. | **Clip ▸ Speed Up Typing…**, or **Speed up typing** in the panel |
| [Auto Zoom](/recording/auto-zoom/) | The typing marks, to zoom in where you typed. | **Zoom on typing** in **Clip ▸ Auto Zoom…** |

**Show shortcuts** and **Speed up typing** are in the panel's **When it lands:** rows, and they're greyed out unless **Record shortcuts** is ticked, because the cursor file would have no keys for them to use.

## With an agent

`record_screen` records keys when it's asked for them, but it never asks macOS for the permission. Without Input Monitoring it won't start, and it names the System Settings pane, so someone has to grant it in the panel first. It won't record keys from a voice-over or a camera on its own. `get_cursor_events` reads the shortcuts and stretches of typing back. See [Tools: recording and screencasts](/mcp/tools-recording/).

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

</system-reminder>

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — with its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, the only files
  that call `rc_*` (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in the file of its
  area. `ReelCore.swift` holds `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25) and `ReelAgentSocket` (below);
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift` holds the media files the core reads or writes —
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index, #216-R), `ReelCube`,
  `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`, `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18;
  `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), `ReelAV1` and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the
  `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) — `ReelCore+Cursor.swift` holds `ReelCursor`
  (`rc_cursor_open`, `rc_cursor_free`: a cursor file's open, which is its check, spec
  §11 CU-9, CU-15; road map creator-jobs CU1a; and `query`, `rc_cursor_query`'s one
  JSON request, CU2, spec §11 CU-25, and the static `query(_:tracks:project:)`, the
  same call over n tracks with a project (`plan_zooms`, CU-70)) — `ReelCore+Framing.swift`
  holds `SpeakerMatch` and `ReelProject.speakerMatch` (`rc_project_speaker_match`, road map
  creator-jobs VR6b, spec §11 VR-65: the face-to-microphone match Make Vertical's sheet
  confirms) — and `ReelCore+Graphics.swift` the graphics engine's
  wrappers (below), with `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`,
  `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`)
  and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)` (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39) — both pure moves
  out of `ReelCore.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T15); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
  `QualifierProps.swift`'s `ColorQualifierPatch`, beside `ColorQualifier` (its
  `blur`, `blursSelection` and `selectionSigma`, GR-35), `QualifierUniforms`
  (`blurred`, set only by `drawAdjustment`) and the pick's `QualifierSample`
  (GR-13), so a row writes
  only its own key to every selected clip. `word_style` has ONE
  app-side writer, `CaptionLayout.place` (W-10). `ReelAgentSocket` (road map
  14's MC2) wraps `rc_agent_socket_start` / `_release`: `start` throws the
  core's sentence, `release` is the quit's unlink-if-still-ours with no join;
  `answer(_:)` hands the tool callback's answer back through
  `rc_agent_string_create` (CJ0d's T15c), a plain static because the trampoline
  runs on the core's server thread, so `AgentServer.swift` names no `rc_*`.
  The `dictionary` extensions on the property types are
  `OpDictionaries.swift`'s (below).
  The graphics engine's wrappers are `ReelCore+Graphics.swift`'s: `GraphicLibrary` (`addFont`,
  `addAsset`, `rasterize`, `families()`; frozen by its first compile,
  rasterize or `families()`) and
  `GraphicModule` (`compile`, `describeJSON`, `svg`; it holds its library
  strongly); their values `GraphicDiagnostic` (with `.error`, `.noModule`
  and `.of(_:)`, the one spelling of a diagnostic made from a message, a
  missing module or a thrown error), `GraphicFailure` (what a
  `diag_out` failure throws; `err_out` stays `ReelCoreError`) and
  `GraphicRaster` are `CoreValues.swift`'s, with `GraphicUsage`, the byte
  bridges `withByteBuffer` and `withMutableByteBuffer` (G-46's toll; never
  `UnsafeMutablePointer(mutating:)`), `SpeedLimits` (a pure move,
  clean-up batch 2), `ReelCoreError` and `Fps.ffiPair` (G6 phase 5's toll), and
  `CoreJSON` (`value`, `snapTicks`: `clipState`'s and `snapCandidates`' JSON
  halves, clean-up round 3's toll; `array`, `overrides`, C1's tolls; `ExportSize.list`,
  `ExportSettings.decoded`, `ReelAV1.Config.decoded`, `withNonNullBytes`, codec-export C5's
  toll), and C1's
  fix-pass moves: `ReelAV1.Config` / `.Color` (an extension of
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift`'s `ReelAV1`, whose `rc_av1_*` calls stay there), `GraphicDiagnostic.list(json:)`,
  `GraphicFailure.checkSides`, `SpeedLimits.decoded` and the free `withBytes`.
  `MediaDescriptor`, `MediaOriginal`, `mediaURL(for:)`, `originalURL(for:)`,
  `revealURL(for:)` (the original, else the copy), `cursorURL(for:)` (the
  cursor file: its bookmark when it resolves, else the stored path, existing or

**Frozen files.** `EditorViewController.swift`, `TimelineView.swift`,
`PreviewCanvasView.swift`, `AgentServer.swift` are **frozen at current
size**: anything adding more than ~50 lines goes in an extension file
(`EditorViewController+<Feature>.swift`, `TimelineView+<Feature>.swift`,
`AgentServer+<Feature>.swift`) or a new `…SheetController`, and the frozen
file keeps only the wiring — a stored property, a closure assignment, a
validator arm, a draw call. The pieces extension files build on are therefore
internal, not private. Pitfalls: a selector declared `@objc` on an extension
needs NO forward in the frozen file (a second declaration is an error); a
command whose body sits at the foot of a non-extension feature file carries
its validator arm there too, or the item falls through to the closing
`return true`; `handleEditorCharacter`'s bare-key `switch` matches in SOURCE
order, so a bare `case "x"` goes BELOW any modified `case "x" where …`; and
`handleEditorKey` refuses while a sheet is attached, because a sheet is
window-modal and the preview panel's forwarded keys would otherwise reach
the key map behind it.

# app/CLAUDE.md — Swift app rules

Applies to everything under `app/`. Build/verification commands and the FFI
lockstep are in the root `CLAUDE.md`; the full design is
`designs/spec/` (§3–4 the UI, §7.4–7.8 the platform side; its `README.md` is
the index). The
long form of each entry below — why each file is the shape it is, and the
traps its history turned up — is `designs/adr/app-file-history.md` (the
full history, every size toll and measurement, is archived; see its
"Original" line); this file is what governs a file now. Files
are listed by family; a file with a header comment of its own carries its
detail there.

## File map

**The core's edge.**
- `ReelCore.swift` — with its `ReelCore+<Area>.swift` files, the only files
  that call `rc_*` (spec §11 CJ-8 (l)); a new wrapper goes in the file of its
  area. `ReelCore.swift` holds `ReelProject`
  (handle + lazily decoded `ProjectSnapshot`; `json`, `snapshot` and
  `planJSON` are memoised PER HANDLE, so keep handles rather than minting
  them; so is `sourceMap(_:)`, `rc_project_source_map` decoded and checked
  once per handle and clip, SR-20), timecode, snapping (export presets/sizes/settings are
  `ExportValues.swift`'s, a pure move, HDR H-1), `ReelSpeed.limits` (the
  core's speed range and audio ceiling, typed as `SpeedLimits` in
  `CoreValues.swift` — no Swift file types a speed bound), `ReelColor` (`rc_normalise_color`, G-25) and `ReelAgentSocket` (below);
  `ReelCore+MediaFiles.swift` holds the media files the core reads or writes —
  `ReelContainer` (`rc_container_*`, a WebM/Matroska file's index, #216-R), `ReelCube`,
  `ReelHDR10` (`rc_hdr10_peak`, spec §11 HD-6; `av1Peak`, `rc_hdr10_av1_peak`, HD-18;
  `stillPeak`, `rc_hdr10_still_peak`, HD-20), `ReelAV1` and `ReelWebM` (`rc_webm_*`, the
  `av1_webm` writer, spec §11 CX-15) — `ReelCore+Cursor.swift` holds `ReelCursor`
  (`rc_cursor_open`, `rc_cursor_free`: a cursor file's open, which is its check, spec
  §11 CU-9, CU-15; road map creator-jobs CU1a; and `query`, `rc_cursor_query`'s one
  JSON request, CU2, spec §11 CU-25, and the static `query(_:tracks:project:)`, the
  same call over n tracks with a project (`plan_zooms`, CU-70)) — `ReelCore+Framing.swift`
  holds `SpeakerMatch` and `ReelProject.speakerMatch` (`rc_project_speaker_match`, road map
  creator-jobs VR6b, spec §11 VR-65: the face-to-microphone match Make Vertical's sheet
  confirms) — and `ReelCore+Graphics.swift` the graphics engine's
  wrappers (below), with `ReelGraphicPackage` (`rc_graphic_package_write`, G-46; `read`,
  `rc_graphic_package_read`, G-47), `GraphicLibrary.usage()` (`rc_graphic_library_usage`)
  and `GraphicLibrary.imageCache(limit:)` (`rc_graphic_image_cache`, G-39) — both pure moves
  out of `ReelCore.swift` (road map creator-jobs CJ0d, T15); `ReelCoreError`, `Fps.ffiPair` and `ReelTime`'s
  seconds conversions are `CoreValues.swift`'s (G6 phase 5's toll T2 and speed ramps SR4-0,
  pure moves); the typed patches are `TypedPatches.swift`'s (`VideoPatch`,
  `AudioPatch`, `ClipPatch`, the `ActionPatch` extension; a pure move, B73),
  `TextPatch` (with `case`, `words` and `word_style`) is `TextPatch.swift`'s,
  moved out so it could grow, and `ShapePatch` `ShapePatch.swift`'s (a pure
  move, the toll for `ReelColor`). `VideoPatch.color` is a sparse `ColorPatch`
  (`GradeProps.swift`, which holds `ColorAdjust` (moved out of
  `ProjectSnapshot.swift`, grading-2 G2-0) with its neutrality helpers, and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(tone:)`, and the wheels' `ColorWheel`, `ColorWheels`,
  `ColorWheelPatch`, `ColorWheelsPatch`, `ColorWheelKind` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(wheels:)` (GR-11)); `VideoPatch.curves` is
  `CurveProps.swift`'s `ColorCurvesPatch`, beside `CurvePoint`,
  `CurveDomain`, `CurveChannel`, `CurveBlend` (a channel blended inside an
  action, spec §11 GR-34; `ColorCurves.blends`, never encoded), `ColorCurves` and
  `LayerUniforms.apply(curves:)` (GR-12, the hue curves GR-32; a
  pure move out of `GradeProps.swift`, grading-4 T4-0); `VideoPatch.qualifier` is
